# Zyke

> Zyke was an AI marketing agent built by three people at IIT Kharagpur between
> July and November 2024. You gave it a brand. It read the brand's website and
> social accounts, worked out how the brand talked, watched what was trending
> that morning, decided by itself which trends were worth reacting to and how to
> bend them toward that brand, and produced finished social posts with generated
> images. If an image was wrong you pointed at the part you wanted changed and
> typed a sentence. The company stopped in November 2024. zyke.in is the archive.

This file is a complete plain-text record of everything on https://zyke.in, for
search engines, researchers and AI agents. Everything here is public and
intended to be read, quoted and trained on. Contact: founders@zyke.in

- Site: https://zyke.in
- Demo video: https://youtu.be/_z__HdAyjl8 (4 minutes, recorded November 2024)
- Code, frontend: https://github.com/zykelabs/zyke-frontend
- Code, backend: https://github.com/zykelabs/zyke-backend
- Tasmay P. Tibrewal: https://www.linkedin.com/in/tasmay-tibrewal/
- Rupam Mahato: https://www.linkedin.com/in/rupammahato/
- Company page: https://www.linkedin.com/company/zykelabs/

## 1. The demo

Four minutes, from a blank brand to edited posts. Recorded in November 2024 on
the version 1.0 build. The example brand is Zomato, an Indian food delivery
company known for cheeky marketing.

Chapters:

- 0:00 The landing page and the three promises
- 0:33 Creating a brand voice, with Zomato as the example
- 1:05 Picking a topic: a trend, or a blog or post to repurpose
- 1:28 A live trend: SpaceX catches a Starship booster
- 1:45 Zyke proposes ideas; you pick, or add your own
- 2:16 Generating the posts: captions and two or three images each
- 2:55 Editing an image by clicking on it and typing a prompt
- 3:41 Original and edited, side by side

That single run produced thirteen images from one trend about a rocket landing.

## 2. The problem

Both founders ran PR and marketing for the Indian Case Challenge at IIT
Kharagpur in 2024, one of the larger business case competitions in Asia. They
needed a lot of posts, fast, and everything available was either expensive or
bad. That is the whole reason Zyke existed.

1. **Agencies cost too much.** A branding agency was out of reach for most of
   the companies we spoke to. The cheap alternatives were generic and still took
   a lot of back and forth to get anything usable.
2. **The AI tools did not sound like you.** Everything on the market wrote in
   the same flat register. It missed what the brand was actually about, so what
   came out was off-brand in a way that was hard to fix.
3. **In-house teams were guessing.** Trial and error, one post at a time. By the
   time a team had something ready, the trend it was chasing had moved on.

Core need: one tool that was efficient, affordable and actually personal to the
brand.

## 3. The promise

Three things the first landing page said. All three shipped.

**I. It aligned the AI with your brand voice.** Zyke researched the brand first:
website, social accounts, anything you uploaded. From that it wrote a voice
profile with tone, emotion and character, which you could correct and save.
Every later output was written through that profile rather than a model's
default register.

**II. It let you edit generated content with precise prompts.** You clicked a
region of an image. A segmentation model proposed what you might have meant. You
confirmed and typed the change. Only that region was repainted; the rest of the
image stayed as it was.

**III. It made content from what was trending.** Live trends arrived with a
short explanation of why each was trending, then were bent toward the brand. A
rocket landing became a post about delivery precision because that is what the
brand's voice cared about.

### How we compared ourselves, December 2024

Against three competitors, left to right: Zyke, Tool A, Tool B, Tool C. The
three rivals are unnamed here, two are still trading, and this comparison is
two years old, so treat it as a record of what we believed at the time.

| Feature | Zyke | A | B | C |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trend analysis | yes | no | no | no |
| Personalised content generation | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Brand voice | yes | yes | no | no |
| Repurpose existing content | yes | yes | no | no |
| Prompt-based image editing | yes | no | no | no |
| Image generation | yes | yes | no | yes |

## 4. How it worked

One brand, one trend, nine posts, one edit. The product was a pipeline. Each
stage handed a richer object to the next: a brand, then an idea, then a post,
then a corrected image. You could stop and steer at every stage.

**Step 1. Brand research and voice.** You entered the brand's name, links and a
few sentences. Zyke read the public footprint with vision and language models
and produced a brand voice: tone, emotion and character filters you could adjust
and save. In the demo the brand voice for Zomato came out as: type
product-based, tone playful and quick and a little cheeky, emotion delight and
mild chaos, character the witty friend who always knows where to eat, sources
zomato.com plus @zomato on Instagram and X plus three uploaded posts.

**Step 2. Ideas from what is trending.** The idea generator listed live trends
with a one-paragraph explanation of each. You could pick one, paste a blog or
Instagram URL to repurpose, or type a topic. Zyke returned several ideas in the
brand's voice for you to tick, and a checkbox let it add one idea of its own.
Trending that day: SpaceX catching a Starship booster with the launch tower.

**Step 3. Posts with images, in the brand's voice.** Three ideas became nine
posts, each with two or three images following a small storyline. Captions came
from a reasoning model prompted with the brand voice. Images came from a FLUX
diffusion model, one per beat of the story.

**Step 4. Point, describe, done.** Click on the image, confirm the region the
segmenter proposes, describe the change. In the demo: "Make the background
darker and add a galaxy with some planets." An inpainting model repainted only
that region. The scooter, the rider and the pizza box were untouched.

## 5. Features

Thirteen things it did, as listed on the product demo.

1. **Brand research and profiling.** Read the brand's site and socials, then
   describe who it is and who it talks to.
2. **Brand voice creation.** Tone, emotion and character filters derived from
   real content, editable and saved per brand.
3. **Customer profile mapping.** Who the audience is, what they respond to,
   where they are.
4. **User engagement tracking.** How posts performed, fed back into what gets
   generated next.
5. **Dashboard with custom metrics.** The numbers a marketing team watches, not
   a generic analytics panel.
6. **Trending topics, tailored to the brand.** Live trends, explained, then bent
   toward the brand.
7. **Personalised brand recommendations.** What to post, when, and why, based on
   the voice and the audience.
8. **Content generation engine.** Text, images and video, generated in one pass
   from a chosen idea.
9. **Content editing pipelines.** Restyle text or images with a sentence;
   click-to-segment editing for precise changes. A Canva-style editor was next
   on the roadmap.
10. **Video storyboards.** Shot-by-shot outlines for short video, in the same
    voice as the posts.
11. **Moodboarding.** A visual direction for a campaign before any post is made.
12. **Post attention analysis.** Where the eye goes on a generated image, and
    whether that is where the message is.
13. **Post-generation content analysis.** A second pass over generated content,
    checking it against the brand voice and the goal.

## 6. What it made

Real output from the testing months, for Zomato, Bira 91, Nike and a coding
school. We did not write any of it. Zyke read the day's trends, picked one,
decided by itself how to bend it toward the brand, wrote the caption and
generated the picture. At most we handed it a brand name and a website.

All of it was generated in the second half of 2024, before any model could spell
reliably or hold more than a megapixel. The misspellings inside the images are
the model's and have not been touched.

### The leaps it made on its own

A headline is not a post. Getting from one to the other is the whole job, and
this is the part nobody wrote down for it.

- **The US government released its files on unidentified objects** (Zomato).
  Declassified alien files were the story of the week. Zyke decided that if
  aliens are real then they are a market, and started writing posts about
  serving them. The asteroid fries and the galaxy sauce are its words.
- **The Prime Minister was all over the Indian news** (Zomato). It read the
  domestic news cycle, saw one name in most of it, and concluded that the move
  was a national endorsement. Nobody asked it for a politician. It also invented
  the hashtag, and then reused that hashtag consistently across a whole
  campaign.
- **SpaceX caught a Starship booster with the launch tower** (Zomato). The trend
  everyone was posting about. Its angle was that catching a hundred-tonne
  booster and getting an order right are the same claim about precision, and it
  pushed that until it had built a bar chart of it.
- **Delhi traffic** (Zomato). The least exotic trend it ever picked, and the
  closest to the product. If the city cannot move, the interesting thing about a
  delivery company is that its riders still do.
- **Indian brands going abroad** (Bira 91). It read the export story in the
  business press and turned it into a travel series, planting the same bottle in
  a different skyline each time.
- **Basketball season** (Nike). A different category entirely. It went for
  shallow depth of field on the product with the athlete deliberately out of
  focus behind, which is how that category actually shoots.

### It got better fast

The same pipeline, three months apart. We did not keep dates against the files,
but the resolution went up every time we rebuilt the image stage, so the size of
a picture is a rough stamp for when it was made.

**September 2024, 512 x 512. It could compose. It could not write.** The early
runs. Zyke already had the interesting part working: it found a trend, made the
leap to the brand and built a picture around it. What it could not do was put a
legible word on the canvas. Headlines came out as letter-shaped noise, and
anything that needed a chart or a label fell apart completely.

Seven images: a rider lifting off Earth on a pizza-fuelled exhaust trail, which
is the picture edited in the demo; a scooter watching a rocket leave with the
delivery box strapped to it; a delivery mission control room with fourteen
screens and not one readable word; an attempt at a data story about delivery
milestones; a Bira 91 bottle between the Statue of Liberty and the Eiffel Tower;
a split citrus product shot with three illegible feature callouts; and a myth
versus fact panel arguing that beer is not only for men, which Zyke picked as an
argument by itself.

**October 2024, 512 to 1024. Headlines start landing.** We rewrote the pipeline
this month: image prompts now came out of the brand voice rather than the
caption, and we moved to FLUX 1.1 Pro. Short headlines and logos start coming
out correctly. Body copy and anything small still collapses, so Zyke was at its
best when it had one line to say.

Twelve images, including: "How space delivers boosters, how Zomato delivers your
pizza, same precision, different missions", with every word correct; a bar chart
comparing booster recovery to order accuracy where the bar labels are right and
the headline is not; four aliens in orbit arguing over asteroid fries and galaxy
sauce with a perfect Zomato wordmark; an invented newspaper front page
announcing Operation Zomato Feast; a four-panel campaign around a hashtag it
made up, its first run at 1024 px; a man with the moon for a head feeding
someone dinner, the strangest thing Zyke ever produced; two Diwali glasses in
front of a blurred rangoli; six Bira 91 bottles on a Stars and Stripes; a myth
and fact carousel with invented calorie numbers; "Brewing The Perfect Code" for
a coding school, spelled exactly right; and a Nike shoe spec sheet where the
product name lands and the specifications are decorative.

**November 2024, 1024 to 1600. This is where it becomes consistent.** Version
1.0. Full sentences hold, logos are right, faces are deliberate, and the same
idea run twice comes back looking like the same campaign rather than two
accidents. This is the month the output stopped being a demo of a pipeline and
started looking like work a brand could actually post.

Sixteen images, including: a smart routing card with every word correct twice in
two type treatments plus a clean logo lockup; a traffic comparison with correct
headline and correct branding on the box; a red scooter throwing sparks past
India Gate at sunset with one letter wrong in the whole picture; the sharpest
thing it ever made, a national endorsement at 1600 px with a hashtag of its own
invention; the same idea held in a square crop for a feed, with composition,
lighting and headline intact across both formats; a 3D cartoon treatment of the
same campaign with headline and sub-line both correct; a four-panel beauty
collage on a real grid with consistent type; and three Nike images including one
where the athlete is deliberately thrown out of focus behind the product.

**The same idea, twice, minutes apart.** By November you could ask for a thing
twice and get the same campaign back. Two runs of a two-panel post exist minutes
apart. In the first, the left panel is clean and the right panel is still
inventing words. In the second, the layout, palette and joke are identical, both
headlines are correct and both boxes are correctly branded. That pair is the
clearest single piece of evidence for the jump.

### Disclaimer

Everything in the gallery is machine generated and was made in 2024 to test a
product. Zomato, Bira 91 and Nike appear as example brands. None of these
companies was involved, none endorsed any of it, and none of it was ever
published on their behalf. Several pictures are Zyke's own attempt at a public
figure, which it reached for without being asked. They are kept because they are
a true record of what the thing did.

## 7. Who it was for

Three sizes of company, three different reasons to want it. Before much code was
written we sat down with marketing people and founders and asked what they
actually needed. These are their words, from those conversations in 2024.

**Small firms.** Need: posts on trending topics, cheap enough to run every week.
"We can give better services than UC but their brand is too big; they have funds
large enough to afford crazy branding." — Mayank Arya, founder

**Medium companies.** Need: brand-relevant content, produced often enough to
grow visibility. "I would give you anything if you can give me better KPIs with
measures on how to improve them." — Akash Walia, marketing manager

**Large companies.** Need: creative work that moves brand positioning, not just
fills a calendar. "We are a one stop solution, but we need to know what the
customer is looking at majorly, so we can show that." — Harshvardhan Chauhan,
former CMO, retail

## 8. The numbers

Zyke was pay as you go. Five dollars of credits on sign-up, then twenty cents a
post. We knew our costs to the cent because every generation was a metered API
call.

- **$0.05** what one generated post cost us. Model calls and storage for a
  single image.
- **$0.20** what we charged for it. Pay as you go, once the free credits ran out.
- **$0.70** one brand voice, once. Research, vision calls and the profile write-up.
- **$5.00** free credits on sign-up. Enough to make a real campaign before paying.

The market, as we sized it in December 2024:

- **$30.34B** total market we were sizing against
- **$2.2B** the slice we could actually serve
- **36.2%** growth rate for AI in social media, to 2032
- **₹208 cr** spent on digital media by about a million Indian SMEs
- 600+ D2C brands in India worth $100B by 2025

What marketers were already using AI for: 33% generate ideas and inspiration,
28% write copy and content, 26% create marketing images. All three were things
Zyke did in one pass, which is the argument the whole deck rested on.

## 9. Under the hood

Three of us built and operated it. There was never one model; each job went to
the model that was good at it, and a saved brand voice object was passed into
every prompt to hold the whole thing together.

### Remember what 2024 was like

Every picture on the site was generated in the second half of 2024, which in
image models is a very long time ago.

- There was no Nano Banana and no GPT Image. There was no model you could hand a
  picture and a sentence to and get the picture back, changed.
- Image models could not write. Any text in a picture came out as approximate
  letter shapes.
- A megapixel was the ceiling. 1024 by 1024 was a good day.
- Instruction following was weak. A long prompt with several requirements in it
  would get two of them.
- Nothing kept a character, a product or a layout consistent between two runs,
  so a set of images that told one story had to be forced.

So a good part of the product was scaffolding around models that were not yet
good enough.

### The trend engine and recommender

Generating a post is the easy half. Deciding what is worth posting about today,
for this brand and not for any other, is the half that made it a product. All of
this is in the archived backend.

1. **Pull what the country is actually searching.** Google Trends daily trending
   searches for India, through pytrends, on an IST clock. Not a hashtag scrape.
   The queries people were typing that morning. Cached six hours.
2. **Ask why each one is trending.** A trending search on its own is a noun with
   no story. Every trend went to Perplexity with one job: explain why this is
   trending right now, not what it is in general, and if there are several
   reasons give all of them. It came back as a one-line summary and a long
   description. That distinction mattered, because a brand cannot react to a
   topic, only to a reason.
3. **Score every trend against the brand.** The scorer received three things:
   the company research database, an analysis of the brand's own historical
   posts, and the full trend list with explanations. It returned a relevance
   score from 1 to 10 for each trend and a ranking, along with the trend's
   original position so the ranking could be mapped back to the source list.
   Scores of 7 to 10 meant directly aligned with high engagement potential, 4 to
   6 partial alignment, 1 to 3 minimal alignment.
4. **Score differently depending on the brand.** This is the part that made it
   feel personal. The instruction split brands in two. A brand whose history
   showed it was creative and willing to be strange got encouraged toward
   unconventional ideas even from trends with nothing to do with its sector. A
   traditional brand got directly related, conventional ideas and was actively
   discouraged from the leaps. The same trend list handed to two brands came
   back ranked differently and used differently.
5. **Turn the ranked trends into ideas, not posts.** For each trend that scored
   well it produced several named ideas with descriptions, still in the brand's
   voice, and stopped there. You saw the ranking, the reasoning and the ideas,
   and chose. A checkbox let it add one idea of its own that you had not asked
   for, which is where a good deal of the stranger output came from.
6. **Cache it, and do not charge for it.** Trends were cached globally for six
   hours and a user's ranked ideas for six hours more. The cost of fetching and
   explaining trends was logged against a house account instead of the user's
   credits, because nobody should pay to find out what is happening.

### From an idea to the images

1. **One idea becomes several image prompts.** The reasoning model was asked for
   a post as XML, with a caption and a list of image prompts inside it, and told
   to vary how many images each post got. That is how the images in a post form
   a sequence instead of three versions of the same picture. Structured output
   was not reliable in 2024, so every prompt asked for XML tags and we parsed
   them by hand.
2. **The brand voice goes in as its own message.** Not a line in a system
   prompt. A saved record with the company research, the tone, emotion and
   character filters, and an analysis of the brand's own past posts, injected as
   a separate system message on every single call. It is the reason two brands
   given the same trend came back with different posts.
3. **Images generated four at a time.** FLUX 1.1 Pro through Together AI, fifty
   steps, at four and a bit cents an image. Requests went out in batches of four
   with a pause between them to stay inside the rate limit, then every image was
   downloaded and inlined so a post travelled as one object.

### The editing pipeline: four workflows and a model choosing between them

This is the part that did not exist anywhere else at the time. There was no
model you could hand a picture and a sentence to, so we built the behaviour out
of a router and four separate pipelines. Most of it ran as a GPU service
alongside the API, and that service is the one piece of Zyke not preserved in
the repos, so this account comes from the calls the app made into it rather than
from the source.

1. **A model decides what kind of edit this is.** You typed a sentence. Before
   anything touched the picture, the image and the available workflows went to
   o1-mini, which decided what you actually wanted and called the tools to do
   it. Change the whole mood, replace one object, delete one object, restyle the
   entire image: these are four different pipelines with different failure
   modes, and picking the wrong one produces garbage. The router picked,
   triggered the workflow and managed it through to the end.
2. **Route one: click to segment, at the granularity you meant.** If you pointed
   at something, one click went to a granularity-controllable interactive
   segmentation model, GraCo, in the same family as Semantic SAM. A single click
   is ambiguous by nature: clicking a rider's jacket could mean the jacket, the
   rider, or the rider and the scooter together. So it returned several masks at
   several granularities for that one click, and you picked the one that matched
   what you meant. That region was then cut out of the image and refilled,
   either by infill or by image to image on the masked area.
3. **Route two: no target, so change everything.** A prompt about the whole
   picture, like making the background darker, has no object to find. That went
   straight to image to image over the full frame with your sentence as the
   instruction, which keeps the composition and moves the look.
4. **Route three: find the thing you named.** If your sentence named an object
   rather than pointing at one, an open-vocabulary detector took over. Grounding
   DINO was given the noun phrase from your prompt and returned candidate
   regions for it. The most related one was selected, converted to a mask, and
   then operated on. Modify meant image to image inside that mask. Remove meant
   infill, so the model had to invent what belonged behind the thing that was
   deleted rather than smearing it.
5. **Route four: restyle the whole thing with a LoRA.** Asking for a different
   look is not an edit to a region, it is an edit to everything at once. We kept
   a set of styling LoRAs, and a style request triggered the matching one and
   re-rendered the image through it. Prompt-only restyling in 2024 tended to
   redraw the picture into something else; a LoRA held the content and moved the
   treatment.
6. **Show the mask before spending anything.** Masks are unreadable as raw
   arrays, so each candidate was dilated with a seventeen by seventeen kernel,
   resized to the picture and alpha-blended over it in colour. You chose from a
   row of previews of your own image with the region lit up. That step ran
   locally with OpenCV and cost nothing, so you could hunt for the right region
   for free and only pay when you committed.
7. **Always edit the original, never the last result.** Every operation was
   applied to the pristine image rather than to the previous edit, with the
   whole chain kept as history you could step back through. Repeated edits in
   2024 degraded fast, each pass softening and shifting what the one before it
   had done. Going back to the original each time is why five edits still looked
   like one picture.
8. **Fight the inpainting model into blending.** Infill liked to hand back a
   half-filled hole, a hard seam, or a caption written into the gap. So the
   instruction was wrapped in a fixed demand to blend the region with the rest
   of the image and fill it completely, plus a long negative prompt listing
   every failure we had seen: empty part, blank image, text, any text,
   alphabets, part not blended with the rest.

### What was actually new about it

- A reasoning model routing image edits by tool call, deciding whether your
  sentence meant a region, an object, the whole frame or the style, a year
  before agentic image editing was a normal idea.
- One click returning several masks at several granularities, so the model asked
  what you meant instead of guessing.
- Open-vocabulary detection wired to the prompt, so you could name a thing you
  had not clicked and have it found, changed or deleted.
- Style handled by LoRAs rather than by prompt, so a restyle kept the picture
  instead of redrawing it.
- Candidate masks shown as previews on your own image, free to browse, so a
  segmentation model became usable by a marketing person.
- Every edit applied to the original rather than the last result, with full undo
  history, so passes did not compound.
- Trends scored per brand from the brand's own history, with creative brands
  pushed toward the leaps and traditional brands pushed away from them.
- Trends explained before being ranked, because a brand can react to a reason
  but not to a noun.
- Trend, idea and post as three separate stages you could stop and steer
  between, each parsed from tagged output.
- Every generation metered to the cent, with trend research billed to a house
  account instead of the user.

Point-and-describe image editing is a checkbox feature now. In November 2024 it
took a reasoning model routing tool calls across four pipelines, two vision
models, a set of LoRAs, a GPU we rented, and a negative prompt written by trial
and error.

### Everything that ran

- **Web app.** Next.js 14, TypeScript, Tailwind. Email sign-up with one-time
  codes. Razorpay wallet for credits.
- **API.** Flask on AWS EC2 in Mumbai behind gunicorn. MongoDB for users, brand
  voices, posts and transactions. Eleven blueprints, twenty-seven routes.
- **Trends and recommendation.** Google Trends daily searches for India through
  pytrends. Perplexity Sonar to explain why each topic is trending. OpenAI
  o1-mini to score and rank trends per brand. Six-hour caches, billed to a house
  account.
- **Language models.** OpenAI o1-mini for ranking, ideas, captions and edit
  routing. Llama 3.1 and GPT-4o mini with vision for brand research. Gemini 1.5
  Flash for repurposing URLs.
- **Image generation.** FLUX 1.1 Pro through Together AI, fifty steps, batches
  of four with a hand-rolled rate limiter.
- **Image editing.** GraCo granularity-controllable interactive segmentation on
  a GPU. Grounding DINO for open-vocabulary object detection. Styling LoRAs for
  whole-image restyling. Stability AI inpainting and image to image. OpenCV
  locally for mask dilation and previews.
- **Data.** Instagram and web scraping for brand research. Google Cloud Storage
  for media. Google Cloud Run and Modal for the GPU services.

The path of one post: trend, why, rank, ideas, captions, images, route, segment,
edit.

## 10. The story

Three people, five months, one Flask route to version 1.0.

It started at IIT Kharagpur, in the campus Business Club. Two of us ended up
running PR and marketing for the Indian Case Challenge. Somewhere in the middle
of that, doing design work at two in the morning, the idea for Zyke stopped
being a joke. Rupam joined in October 2024 and wrote most of the product you can
see in the demo.

It started in July 2024 as a single page and a single API route: type a brief,
answer two clarifying questions, get posts and images back. It was rough. People
used it anyway.

By October we had learned what mattered. The brand voice had to be a real, saved
object rather than a text box. Trends had to be live. Images had to be fixable
without regenerating everything. So we rewrote it: a proper web app, an API with
a database, accounts, and a segmentation model on a GPU so you could click the
part of the picture you wanted changed.

Version 1.0 shipped on 5 November 2024 and the demo was recorded on it. Bira 91
and a handful of other companies tested it. It did not go further than that.

Timeline:

- **July 2024** Version zero. One Flask route, one hand-written page, a
  five-stage prompt chain on Claude 3.5 Sonnet and FLUX. Live at www.zyke.in.
- **August 2024** Posts split per platform. Newer image model. Source shared
  with a second builder.
- **October 2024** Rewritten in three weeks: Next.js app, Flask and MongoDB
  API, accounts, brand voice, trends, repurposing, payments.
- **November 2024** Version 1.0. Click-to-segment image editing on a GPU
  service. The demo was recorded.
- **2025** The company wound down. The domain, the code and this page remain.

### Who built it

- **Tasmay P. Tibrewal**, CTO turned CEO. https://www.linkedin.com/in/tasmay-tibrewal/
- **Rupam Mahato**, founding engineer. https://www.linkedin.com/in/rupammahato/
- **Siddharth Dikshit**, co-founder and CEO until November. Left after the dispute.

Between us we had won gold at Inter IIT for product development and for an NLP
problem statement, which is roughly how we convinced ourselves we could build
this in the first place.

### What paid for it

$50k+ in credits, across seven programmes. No cash.

| Programme | Amount | For |
|---|---|---|
| Y Combinator | $25,000 | Startup school credits across cloud and tooling |
| Modal Labs | $11,000 | GPU credits to serve the segmentation model |
| Daytona | $10,000 | Development environment credits |
| CampusFund | $5,000 | AWS credits to build the MVP |
| Google Cloud for Startups | $2,000 | Cloud Run and storage |
| Microsoft for Startups | $1,000 | Azure credits |
| MongoDB for Startups | $500 | Database credits |

Every model call behind every picture on the site was paid for out of that.

## 11. Why we started it, and why it stopped

Worth writing down honestly, because the interesting part of a company that did
not work is usually not the technology.

### What we were actually trying to build

1. **The posts were never the point.** Zyke was the first step toward a content
   pipeline that ran itself. Not a tool you open and prompt every morning, but
   an engine that knew a brand well enough to keep producing for it without
   being asked.
2. **Two engines were supposed to do that.** A trend engine that watched what was
   happening and decided what was worth reacting to. And a brand engine that
   went and read everything: hundreds of pages of a company's own site, its
   whole back catalogue of posts, how it styles its images, who it talks to,
   what it has already said. Not a prompt describing a brand. A researched model
   of one.
3. **The far end of it was not marketing.** Once you can generate on-brand
   images and video from a researched model of a style, marketing is only the
   easiest customer. The same machinery points at entertainment. Something in
   the shape of what Higgsfield is doing now for generated video, with a trend
   engine and a brand research engine bolted on the front. That was the
   direction, and we were nowhere near it.
4. **And I wanted to build something.** Honestly, that is half the answer. I came
   into college too techy and too ambitious to sit still. I wanted to ship
   things, start a company, hack on hard problems and have fun doing it. Zyke was
   that as much as it was a business.

### Why it did not work

We built the thing and never did the other half.

1. We did not reach out enough. We should have been in front of brands every
   week. We were not.
2. We never properly understood what a marketing team needs day to day. We did
   not do enough customer research, so most decisions came out of our own
   guesses.
3. We could not sell. There was a working product and a demo people liked, and
   nothing behind it.
4. We never got real pilots running. A few companies tried it. That is not the
   same as one brand using it every week and telling you what is broken.
5. Everything we were good at sat on one side of the business. The other side
   stayed empty.

Then there were co-founder disputes, and with the outreach already stalled there
was not much holding it together. It ended there. I was in my third year and
left for an internship. The lesson is not subtle: building the hard part turned
out not to be the hard part.

---

## The repositories

- Frontend and this page: https://github.com/zykelabs/zyke-frontend
- Flask and MongoDB API: https://github.com/zykelabs/zyke-backend

`main` is this archive page: a Next.js 14 static export, no backend. The earlier
work is preserved as branches rather than deleted:

- `legacy/zyke` — the original single-page app, July to October 2024
- `legacy/zyke-team` — an August 2024 fork of it shared with a teammate
- `legacy/zyke-new-2` — the October rewrite, which the app below descends from
- `legacy/zyke-frontend-app` — the full version 1.0 Next.js product
- `legacy/zyke-vercel` — a Vercel deployment experiment

One earlier repo is deliberately not published because it has real credentials
committed in its history; its purged successor, `legacy/zyke-new-2`, is here
instead.
